title: The 48 Laws of Power
author: Robert Greene
translator: A Folio digest: original summaries of each law, with quotes from the public-domain classics behind them. Greene's book is copyrighted — read the full text in print.
blurb: Forty-eight rules of power, from royal courts to modern offices — each law in a minute, paired with a line from Machiavelli, Sun Tzŭ, Gracián or La Rochefoucauld. Know them to use them, or to spot them used on you.

courtier.m: A person who attends a king's court, often seeking favour.
courtier.e: Office courtiers laugh loudest at the boss's jokes.

envy.m: A painful wish to have what someone else has.
envy.e: Her new car filled the neighbours with envy.

envious.m: A painful wish to have what someone else has.
envious.e: Her new car filled the neighbours with envy.

insecurity.m: Not confident; easily worried about your place.
insecurity.e: The insecure manager hated being corrected in meetings.

rival.m: Someone competing with you for the same thing.
rival.e: The two cafés on the street are rivals.

decoy.m: Something used to distract or mislead.
decoy.e: The empty box on the porch was a decoy for parcel thieves.

mystique.m: An air of mystery that makes someone fascinating.
mystique.e: The chef never gives interviews, which adds to her mystique.

reputation.m: What people generally think of you.
reputation.e: One rude review can dent a café's reputation.

indispensable.m: So needed that you cannot do without it.
indispensable.e: The only person who knows the old billing system is indispensable.

self-interest.e: Free samples work because they appeal to self-interest.

unpredictable.e: The weather this week is unpredictable — carry an umbrella.

scapegoat.m: Someone blamed for the mistakes of others.
scapegoat.e: The intern became the scapegoat for the manager's error.

illusion.m: Something that seems real but is not.
illusion.e: The mirror wall gives the illusion of a bigger room.

fantasy.m: Something imagined, often too good to be true.
fantasy.e: Getting rich overnight is a fantasy most ads sell.

dignity.m: Self-respect and a calm, worthy manner.
dignity.e: She lost the match with dignity, shaking every hand.

provoke.m: To deliberately make someone react, often angrily.
provoke.e: Don't provoke the dog by pulling its tail.

successor.m: The person who comes after someone in a role.
successor.e: The founder's successor struggled to fill his shoes.

predecessor.m: The person who held a role before.
predecessor.e: Her predecessor left the files in a mess.

complacent.m: Too satisfied to see danger coming.
complacent.e: The leading team grew complacent and lost in the last minute.

ostracism.m: Being shut out of a group on purpose.
ostracism.e: Ancient Athens used ostracism to exile powerful men for ten years.

cards.chTitle: Never Outshine the Master
cards.title: Let the boss shine
cards.text: People above you want to feel superior. If you look more brilliant than them, you stir envy and insecurity. In 1661 Nicolas Fouquet threw a party so dazzling that King Louis XIV felt upstaged — within weeks Fouquet was arrested and spent the rest of his life in prison. Make your superiors look good; let your talent serve them.
cards.quote: All victories breed hate, and that over your superior is foolish or fatal.
cards.orig: All victories breed hate, and that over your superior is foolish or fatal. Superiority is always detested, 4 fortiori superiority over superiority. Caution can gloss over common advantages ; for example, good looks may be cloaked by careless attire. There be some that will grant you precedence in good luck or good temper, but none in good sense, least of all a prince ; for good sense is a royal prerogative, any claim to that is a case of /ése majesté. They are princes, and wish to be so in that most princely of qualities. ‘They will allow aman to help them but not to surpass them, and will have any advice tendered them appear like a recollection of something they have forgotten rather than as a guide to something they cannot find. The stars teach us this Jinesse with happy tact; though they are his

cards.qLife: Correcting your manager in front of the client may cost you the next promotion.

cards.chTitle: Never Outshine the Master
cards.title: In history: Fouquet's party
cards.text: In 1661 Nicolas Fouquet, France's finance minister, threw a dazzling party at his new château for the young Louis XIV. Fireworks, a new Molière play, gold plates. The king felt outshone. Within weeks Fouquet was arrested, and he died in prison. Louis later built Versailles, bigger than anything Fouquet had.
cards.quote: Never seem wiser, nor more learned, than the people you are with.
cards.qMean: Don't act cleverer or grander than those around you.
cards.qLife: Showing up the boss in a meeting can cost you more than the idea was worth.
cards.orig: There is another species of learned men, who, though less dogmatical and supercilious, are not less impertinent. These are the communicative and shining pedants, who adorn their conversation, even with women, by happy quotations of Greek and Latin; and who have contracted such a familiarity with the Greek and Roman authors, that they, call them by certain names or epithets denoting intimacy. As OLD Homer; that SLY ROGUE Horace; MARO, instead of Virgil; and Naso, Instead of Ovid. These are often imitated by coxcombs, who have no learning at all; but who have got some names and some scraps of ancient authors by heart, which they improperly and impertinently retail in all companies, in hopes of passing for scholars. If, therefore, you would avoid the accusation of pedantry on one hand, or the suspicion of ignorance on the other, abstain from learned ostentation. Speak the language of the company that you are in; speak it purely, and unlarded with any other. Never seem wiser, nor more learned, than the people you are with. Wear your learning, like your watch, in a private pocket: and do not pull it out and strike it; merely to show that you have one. If you are asked what o’clock it is, tell it; but do not proclaim it hourly and unasked, like the watchman.

cards.chTitle: Never Put Too Much Trust in Friends, Learn How to Use Enemies
cards.title: Friends and enemies
cards.text: Friends can turn on you quickly because envy hides inside friendship, and they expect favours. A former enemy you win over has more to prove and works harder to show loyalty. Keep an eye on friends; don't be afraid to hire a rival.
cards.quote: A wise man gets more use from his enemies than a fool from his friends.
cards.orig: You should learn to seize things not by the blade, which cuts, but by the handle, which saves you from harm: especially 1s this the rule with the doings of your enemies. A wise man gets more use from his enemies than a fool from his friends. ‘Their ill-will often levels mountains of difficulties which one would otherwise not face. Many have had their greatness made for them by their enemies. Flattery is more dangerous than hatred, because it covers the stains which the other causes to be wiped out. The wise will turn ill-will into a mirror more faithful than that of kindness, and remove or improve the faults referred to. Caution thrives well when rivalry and ill-will are next-door neighbours.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: The Madrid Skylitzes, Byzantine chronicle · public domain
cards.qMean: A smart person learns more from enemies than a fool from friends.
cards.qLife: A harsh online review often teaches a café more than its friends' praise.
cards.link: Don't threaten those above you. And don't trust too easily those beside you.

cards.chTitle: Never Put Too Much Trust in Friends, Learn How to Use Enemies
cards.title: In history: a friend turned killer
cards.text: The Byzantine emperor Michael III raised his friend Basil, a stable groom, to co-emperor. Basil had him murdered and took the throne. Benjamin Franklin found the opposite trick: he turned a rival into a lifelong friend by asking to borrow a book.
cards.quote: He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged.
cards.qMean: People who have helped you once tend to like you more, not less.
cards.qLife: Asking a cold colleague for advice can warm them up.
cards.orig: I therefore did not like the opposition of this new member, who was a gentleman of fortune and education, with talents that were likely to give him, in time, great influence in the House, which, indeed, afterwards happened. I did not, however, aim at gaining his favour by paying any servile respect to him, but, after some time, took this other method. Having heard that he had in his library a certain very scarce and curious book, I wrote a note to him, expressing my desire of perusing that book, and requesting he would do me the favour of lending it to me for a few days. He sent it immediately, and I return'd it in about a week with another note, expressing strongly my sense of the favour. When we next met in the House, he spoke to me (which he had never done before), and with great civility; and he ever after manifested a readiness to serve me on all occasions, so that we became great friends, and our friendship continued to his death. This is another instance of the truth of an old maxim I had learned, which says, "He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged." And it shows how much more profitable it is prudently to remove, than to resent, return, and continue inimical proceedings.
cards.origFrom: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (1791)
cards.qBy: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (1791)

cards.chTitle: Conceal Your Intentions
cards.title: Hide your hand
cards.text: If people know exactly what you want, they can block you. Keep them guessing. Use a decoy goal or a show of sincerity to throw them off. By the time your real aim is clear, it is too late for them to stop it.
cards.quote: It is both useless and insipid to play with the cards on the table.
cards.orig: Admiration at their novelty heightens. the value of your achievements. It is both useless and insipid to play with the cards on the table. If you do not declare yourself immediately, you arouse expectation, especially when the importance of your position makes you the ' object of general attention. Mix a little ‘ mystery with everything, and the very mystery arouses veneration. And when you explairf, be not too explicit, just as you do not expose your inmost thoughts in ordinary intercourse. Cautious silence is the holy of holies of worldly wisdom. A resolution declared is never highly thought of; it only leaves room for criticism. And if it happens to fail, you are doubly unfortunate. Besides you imitate the Divine way when you cause men to wonder and watch.

cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)

cards.qMean: Showing all your plans at once is pointless and boring.
cards.qLife: Announcing your job search to the whole office before you have an offer.
cards.link: Friends can turn. So keep your real plans to yourself.

cards.chTitle: Conceal Your Intentions
cards.title: In history: Bismarck's peace speech
cards.text: In 1850 Otto von Bismarck shocked his colleagues by giving a speech praising peace with Austria, the rival he despised. It won him the post he wanted. Years later, in power, he went to war with Austria and won. Nobody had seen his real plan.
cards.quote: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are
cards.qMean: People see your surface; few know what's underneath.
cards.qLife: A quiet student who nobody expects to top the exam.
cards.orig: For this reason a prince ought to take care that he never lets anything slip from his lips that is not replete with the above-named five qualities, that he may appear to him who sees and hears him altogether merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious. There is nothing more necessary to appear to have than this last quality, inasmuch as men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand, because it belongs to everybody to see you, to few to come in touch with you. Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them; and in the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result.

cards.chTitle: Always Say Less Than Necessary
cards.title: Silence is power
cards.text: The more you talk, the more likely you are to say something foolish, and the more ordinary you seem. Short, vague answers make people wonder what you really think. Powerful people often impress by how little they say.

cards.qMean: Careful silence is the deepest form of practical wisdom.
cards.qLife: In a negotiation, the one who stays quiet longer usually gets the better deal.
cards.link: Hiding your aims starts with your mouth: say less.

cards.chTitle: Always Say Less Than Necessary
cards.title: In history: Coriolanus talks too much
cards.text: Coriolanus was a Roman war hero, and the people were ready to make him consul. Then he started talking, insulting the common people in speech after speech. They turned on him and drove him into exile. His deeds won them; his words lost them.
cards.quote: Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation.
cards.qMean: Only say what helps; skip pointless talk.
cards.qLife: Saying less in a job interview often impresses more than talking nonstop.
cards.orig:
1. Temperance.

Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.

2. Silence.

3. Order.

Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.

4. Resolution.

cards.chTitle: So Much Depends on Reputation — Guard It with Your Life
cards.title: Your name is your shield
cards.text: Reputation works before you even enter the room. A strong one makes people respect and fear you; a damaged one invites attacks. Guard it, notice early threats, and never let one mocking nickname stick to you.
cards.quote: if it clings to you with a nickname, your reputation is in danger.
cards.orig: Many heads go to make the mob, and in each of them are eyes for malice to use and a tongue for detraction to wag. If a single ill report spread, it casts a blemish on your fair fame, and if it clings to you with a nickname, your reputation is in danger. Generally it is some salient defect or ridiculous trait that gives rise to the rumours, At times these are

cards.qMean: Once a mocking nickname sticks, your reputation is in danger.
cards.qLife: A teacher nicknamed 'Snore' struggles to be taken seriously by new classes.
cards.link: What you don't say protects you. What others say about you protects you more: your reputation.

cards.chTitle: So Much Depends on Reputation — Guard It with Your Life
cards.title: In history: guarding a name
cards.text: Julius Caesar divorced his wife Pompeia after a scandal, though he said he believed she was innocent. His reason: Caesar's wife must be above suspicion. He understood that a reputation, once stained, is very hard to clean.
cards.quote: a prince should guard himself, above all things, against being despised and hated
cards.qMean: Above all, a leader must avoid being looked down on or hated.
cards.qLife: One viral bad review can hurt a restaurant more than ten good ones help.
cards.orig: And there is nothing wastes so rapidly as liberality, for even whilst you exercise it you lose the power to do so, and so become either poor or despised, or else, in avoiding poverty, rapacious and hated. And a prince should guard himself, above all things, against being despised and hated; and liberality leads you to both. Therefore it is wiser to have a reputation for meanness which brings reproach without hatred, than to be compelled through seeking a reputation for liberality to incur a name for rapacity which begets reproach with hatred.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)

cards.chTitle: Court Attention at All Costs
cards.title: Be seen
cards.text: People judge by appearances, and what goes unseen is forgotten. Stand out — with a striking style, a mystery, even a little scandal. P. T. Barnum built a business on drawing crowds. Attention brings opportunity; being ignored brings nothing.
cards.quote: Display startling novelties, rise afresh like the sun every day.
cards.orig: … staleness of custom weakens admiration, and a mediocrity that’s new often eclipses the highest excellence grown old. Try therefore to be born again in valour, in genius, in fortune, in all. Display startling novelties, rise afresh like the sun every day. Change too the scene on which you shine, so that your loss may be felt in the old scenes of your triumph, while the novelty of your powers wins you applause in the new.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Life of P. T. Barnum frontispiece 1855 · public domain
cards.qMean: Keep showing something new and surprising, like a sunrise every day.
cards.qLife: Creators who post fresh content keep their audience; those who repeat lose it.
cards.link: A reputation needs fuel. Attention is the fuel.

cards.chTitle: Court Attention at All Costs
cards.title: In history: Barnum's mermaid
cards.text: P. T. Barnum advertised a real 'Fiji mermaid' all over New York. It was a monkey sewn to a fish. Crowds paid to see it anyway, and the arguments about whether it was fake only brought more. Barnum knew attention of any kind could be turned into fame.
cards.quote: affirmation, repetition, and contagion
cards.qMean: Ideas spread by bold statements, repeated, that catch on like a cold.
cards.qLife: A catchy jingle you can't get out of your head.
cards.orig: When, however, it is proposed to imbue the mind of a crowd with ideas and beliefs--with modern social theories, for instance--the leaders have recourse to different expedients. The principal of them are three in number and clearly defined--affirmation, repetition, and contagion. Their action is somewhat slow, but its effects, once produced, are very lasting.
cards.origFrom: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)

cards.title: In history: the inventor and the businessman
cards.text: Nikola Tesla worked for Thomas Edison and solved hard engineering problems, but the credit and the money went elsewhere. Edison ran a workshop where many minds worked under one name. Sun Tzu would have understood: great results come from combined effort, not one exhausted individual.

cards.qMean: A smart leader relies on teamwork rather than demanding everything from one person.

cards.chTitle: Make Other People Come to You — Use Bait if Necessary
cards.title: Make them come to you
cards.text: Whoever acts first, on the other's ground, is at a disadvantage. Lure opponents into coming to you, with a tempting offer if needed. Then you control the place and the rules. Napoleon's enemies, believing him beaten, came to him — and lost.
cards.quote: the clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy, but does not allow the enemy's will to be imposed on him.
cards.orig:
1. Sun Tzŭ said: Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy, will be fresh for the fight; whoever is second in the field and has to hasten to battle, will arrive exhausted.

2. Therefore the clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy, but does not allow the enemy’s will to be imposed on him.

3. By holding out advantages to him, he can cause the enemy to approach of his own accord; or, by inflicting damage, he can make it impossible for the enemy to draw near.

cards.qLife: Choose the meeting place and time yourself instead of fitting someone else's.

cards.chTitle: Win Through Your Actions, Never Through Argument
cards.title: Show, don't argue
cards.text: Winning an argument often makes the loser resent you. Demonstrate instead. When an official insisted a statue's nose was too large, Michelangelo pretended to chip at it, dropping marble dust — and the official was delighted with the 'change'. Results persuade; words provoke.
cards.quote: To dissent from others' views is regarded as an insult
cards.orig: … danger ; only a Socrates can undertake it. To dissent from others’ views is regarded as an insult, because it is their condemnation. Disgust is doubled on account of the thing blamed and of the person who praised it. Truth is for the few, error is both common and vulgar. ‘The wise man is not known by what he says on the house-tops, for there he speaks not with his own voice but with that of common folly, however much his inmost thoughts may gainsay it. The prudent avoid being contradicted as much as contradicting: though they have their censure ready they are not ready to publish it. ‘Thought is free, force cannot and should not be used to it. The wise man therefore retires into silence, and if he allows himself to come out of it, he does so in the shade and before few and fit persons.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Michelango Portrait by Volterra · public domain
cards.qMean: Disagreeing with people's opinions feels like an insult to them.
cards.qLife: Telling a friend their favourite film is bad starts an argument, not a discussion.
cards.link: When they come, don't argue with them. Show them.

cards.chTitle: Win Through Your Actions, Never Through Argument
cards.title: In history: Michelangelo's nose job
cards.text: The mayor of Florence told Michelangelo that his giant David's nose was too big. Michelangelo didn't argue. He climbed up with a little marble dust, pretended to chisel, let the dust fall, and asked, 'Better?' 'Much better,' said the mayor. The statue was unchanged.
cards.quote: I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction to the sentiments of others, and all positive assertion of my own.
cards.qMean: I made it a rule never to contradict people directly or insist I was right.
cards.qLife: Letting a parent think the plan was their idea.
cards.orig: I cannot boast of much success in acquiring the reality of this virtue, but I had a good deal with regard to the appearance of it. I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction to the sentiments of others, and all positive assertion of my own. I even forbid myself, agreeably to the old laws of our Junto, the use of every word or expression in the language that imported a fix'd opinion, such as certainly, undoubtedly, etc., and I adopted, instead of them, I conceive, I apprehend, or I imagine a thing to be so or so; or it so appears to me at present. When another asserted something that I thought an error, I deny'd myself the pleasure of contradicting him abruptly, and of showing immediately some absurdity in his proposition; and in answering I began by observing that in certain cases or circumstances his opinion would be right, but in the present case there appear'd or seem'd to me some difference, etc. I soon found the advantage of this change in my manner; the conversations I engag'd in went on more pleasantly. The modest way in which I propos'd my opinions procur'd them a readier reception and less contradiction; …

cards.chTitle: Infection: Avoid the Unhappy and Unlucky
cards.title: Misery is contagious
cards.text: Some people carry bad luck and bad moods with them, and pull everyone close to them down. Their problems spread like a disease. Don't try to rescue everyone — keep company with the cheerful and the fortunate.

cards.orig: The other and better course is to send colonies to one or two places, which may be as keys to that state, for it is necessary either to do this or else to keep there a great number of cavalry and infantry. And irresolute princes, to avoid present dangers, generally follow the neutral path, and are generally ruined. But when a prince declares himself gallantly in favour of one side, if the party with whom he allies himself conquers, although the victor may be powerful and may have him at his mercy, yet he is indebted to him, and there is established a bond of amity; and men are never so shameless as to become a monument of ingratitude by oppressing you. Victories after all are never so complete that the victor must not show some regard, especially to justice. But if he with whom you ally yourself loses, you may be sheltered by him, and whilst he is able he may aid you, and you become companions on a fortune that may rise again.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Armada Portrait Elizabeth I Queens House · public domain

cards.chTitle: Play a Sucker to Catch a Sucker — Seem Dumber Than Your Mark
cards.title: Look less clever
cards.text: Nobody likes feeling stupid. If you seem a bit slower than others, they relax, and their guard drops. Appearing harmless can be a smart disguise.
cards.quote: there are times when the greatest wisdom lies in seeming not to be wise.
cards.orig: The wisest play this card at times, and there are times when the greatest wisdom lies in seeming not to be wise. You need not be unwise, but merely affect unwisdom. To be wise with fools and foolish with-the wise were of little use. Speak to each in his own language. He is no fool who affects folly, but he is who suffers from it. Ingenuous folly rather than the pretended is the true foolishness, since cleverness has arrived at such a pitch. ‘To be well liked one must dress in the skin of the simplest of animals.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Emperor Claudius, marble bust · public domain
cards.qMean: Sometimes the wisest move is to look less clever than you are.
cards.qLife: Letting the know-it-all explain something you already understand, to keep the peace.
cards.link: Staying free sometimes means looking less clever than you are.

cards.chTitle: Play a Sucker to Catch a Sucker — Seem Dumber Than Your Mark
cards.title: In history: Claudius the fool
cards.text: Claudius stuttered and limped, and his family treated him as a harmless idiot. He survived the murderous reigns of Tiberius and Caligula because no one saw him as a threat. When Caligula was killed, the soldiers made Claudius emperor, and he ruled capably for thirteen years.
cards.quote: Wear your learning, like your watch, in a private pocket
cards.qMean: Keep your cleverness hidden, like a watch in your pocket.
cards.qLife: The quiet employee everyone underestimates who ends up running the company.
cards.orig: There is another species of learned men, who, though less dogmatical and supercilious, are not less impertinent. These are the communicative and shining pedants, who adorn their conversation, even with women, by happy quotations of Greek and Latin; and who have contracted such a familiarity with the Greek and Roman authors, that they, call them by certain names or epithets denoting intimacy. As OLD Homer; that SLY ROGUE Horace; MARO, instead of Virgil; and Naso, Instead of Ovid. These are often imitated by coxcombs, who have no learning at all; but who have got some names and some scraps of ancient authors by heart, which they improperly and impertinently retail in all companies, in hopes of passing for scholars. If, therefore, you would avoid the accusation of pedantry on one hand, or the suspicion of ignorance on the other, abstain from learned ostentation. Speak the language of the company that you are in; speak it purely, and unlarded with any other. Never seem wiser, nor more learned, than the people you are with. Wear your learning, like your watch, in a private pocket: and do not pull it out and strike it; merely to show that you have one. If you are asked what o’clock it is, tell it; but do not proclaim it hourly and unasked, like the watchman.
cards.origFrom: Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son (1774)
cards.qBy: Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son (1774)
cards.cap: Statue of Emperor Claudius in Vatican Museum · public domain

cards.chTitle: Use the Surrender Tactic: Transform Weakness into Power
cards.title: Bend, don't break
cards.text: When you are weaker, don't fight for honour's sake. Give in for now; it buys time, calms the winner, and lets you prepare. Surrender can make an opponent arrogant and careless.
cards.quote: Pretend to be weak, that he may grow arrogant.
cards.orig:
20. Hold out baits to entice the enemy. Feign disorder, and crush him.

21. If he is secure at all points, be prepared for him. If he is in superior strength, evade him.

22. If your opponent is of choleric temper, seek to irritate him. Pretend to be weak, that he may grow arrogant.

23. If he is taking his ease, give him no rest.
cards.origFrom: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.qBy: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.cap: Velazquez-The Surrender of Breda · public domain
cards.qMean: Pretend to be weak so your opponent becomes overconfident.
cards.qLife: Act unsure at the start of a chess game so your rival plays carelessly.
cards.link: Looking weak can be a weapon. So can surrender.

cards.chTitle: Use the Surrender Tactic: Transform Weakness into Power
cards.title: In history: the willow and the oak
cards.text: An old fable: the proud oak stood stiff against the storm and was torn out by the roots; the willow bent to the ground and stood again when the wind passed. The Tao Te Ching puts the same idea in one line: the sage places himself last, and ends up first.
cards.quote: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place
cards.qMean: The wise put themselves last and end up first.
cards.qLife: Apologising first in an argument often earns more respect than winning it.
cards.orig:
2. Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place; he treats his person as if it were foreign to him, and yet that person is preserved. Is it not because he has no personal and private ends, that therefore such ends are realised?

8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.qBy: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Birds flocking at a willow embankment, Xia Shuwen · public domain

cards.chTitle: Concentrate Your Forces
cards.title: Focus
cards.text: Spreading yourself across many goals weakens all of them. Pour your energy into one strong point — one project, one patron, one skill. Depth beats scattered effort.
cards.quote: we can form a single united body, while the enemy must split up into fractions.
cards.orig:
14. We can form a single united body, while the enemy must split up into fractions. Hence there will be a whole pitted against separate parts of a whole, which means that we shall be many to the enemy’s few.

15. And if we are able thus to attack an inferior force with a superior one, our opponents will be in dire straits.
cards.origFrom: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.qBy: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.cap: The House of Rothschild · public domain
cards.qMean: Stay united while forcing the other side to split up.
cards.qLife: A team that sticks together while the other team argues wins the match.
cards.link: Bend when you must; but when you strike, strike in one place.

cards.chTitle: Concentrate Your Forces
cards.title: In history: the Rothschild brothers
cards.text: Mayer Amschel Rothschild sent his five sons to five European cities, but they worked as one family firm, sharing information by private couriers. Concentrated trust made them the most powerful bankers in Europe. Chesterfield's advice to his son is the everyday version: one thing at a time.
cards.quote: There is time enough for everything, in the course of the day, if you do but one thing at once
cards.qMean: If you focus on one thing at a time, you'll find time for everything.
cards.qLife: Turning off notifications to finish one assignment properly.
cards.orig: … A man is fit for neither business nor pleasure, who either cannot, or does not, command and direct his attention to the present object, and, in some degree, banish for that time all other objects from his thoughts. If at a ball, a supper, or a party of pleasure, a man were to be solving, in his own mind, a problem in Euclid, he would be a very bad companion, and make a very poor figure in that company; or if, in studying a problem in his closet, he were to think of a minuet, I am apt to believe that he would make a very poor mathematician. There is time enough for everything, in the course of the day, if you do but one thing at once; but there is not time enough in the year, if you will do two things at a time. The Pensionary de Witt, who was torn to pieces in the year 1672, did the whole business of the Republic, and yet had time left to go to assemblies in the evening, and sup in company. Being asked how he could possibly find time to go through so much business, and yet amuse himself in the evenings as he did, he answered, there was nothing so easy; …
cards.origFrom: Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son (1774)
cards.qBy: Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son (1774)
cards.cap: Anselm Meier von Rothschild (Amschel Mayer Rothschild), Frankfurt a. M. 1773-1855 · public domain

cards.chTitle: Play the Perfect Courtier
cards.title: Master the room
cards.text: Every workplace is a kind of court with its own manners. The skilled courtier never shows off, flatters with care, notices moods, and stays graceful. Respect is earned by giving it.
cards.quote: pay respect that you may be respected, and know that to be esteemed you must show esteem.
cards.orig: There is no occasion to seek dislike: it comes without seeking quickly enough. There are many who hate of their own accord without knowing the why or the how. Their illwill outruns our readiness to please. Their ill-nature is more prone to do others harm than their cupidity is eager to gain advantage for themselves. Some manage to be on bad terms with all, because they always either produce or experience vexation of spirit. Once hate has taken root it is, like bad repute, ditficult to eradicate. Wise men are feared, the malevolent are abhorred, the arrogant are regarded with disdain, buffoons with contempt, eccentrics with neglect. ‘Therefore pay respect that you may be respected, and know that to be esteemed you must show esteem.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Baldassare Castiglione, by Raffaello Sanzio, from C2RMF retouched · public domain
cards.qMean: Respect others if you want respect back.
cards.qLife: Greet the security guard by name and they'll help you when you forget your badge.
cards.link: Focus works at court too. The perfect courtier is focused charm.

cards.chTitle: Play the Perfect Courtier
cards.title: In history: The Book of the Courtier
cards.text: In 1528 Baldassare Castiglione described the perfect courtier: graceful, witty, never showing effort, always pleasing. Kings read it for two hundred years. Chesterfield, writing to his son, agreed that pleasing others is a skill to be learned, and a hard one.
cards.quote: The art of pleasing is a very necessary one to possess; but a very difficult one to acquire.
cards.qMean: Being pleasant to others is important, but hard to learn.
cards.qLife: A great receptionist makes every visitor feel welcome.
cards.orig: DEAR BOY: The art of pleasing is a very necessary one to possess; but a very difficult one to acquire. It can hardly be reduced to rules; and your own good sense and observation will teach you more of it than I can. Do as you would be done by, is the surest method that I know of pleasing. Observe carefully what pleases you in others, and probably the same thing in you will please others. If you are pleased with the complaisance and attention of others to your humors, your tastes, or your weaknesses, depend upon it the same complaisance and attention, on your part to theirs, will equally please them. Take the tone of the company that you are in, and do not pretend to give it; be serious, gay, or even trifling, as you find the present humor of the company; this is an attention due from every individual to the majority. Do not tell stories in company; there is nothing more tedious and disagreeable; if by chance you know a very short story, and exceedingly applicable to the present subject of conversation, tell it in as few words as possible; …
cards.origFrom: Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son (1774)
cards.qBy: Lord Chesterfield, Letters to His Son (1774)
cards.cap: Titian - Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione, c.1536-1538 · public domain

cards.chTitle: Re-Create Yourself
cards.title: Write your own role
cards.text: Don't accept the identity others hand you. Shape your own image, like an actor building a character. Julius Caesar and many others crafted public personas. Keep renewing yourself so you never grow stale.
cards.quote: Renew your Brilliance. 'Tis the privilege of the Phoenix.
cards.orig: Renew your Brilliance. 'Tis the privilege of the Phoenix. Ability is wont to grow old, and with it fame. The staleness of custom weakens admiration, and a mediocrity that's new often eclipses the highest excellence grown old. Try therefore to be born again in valour, in genius, in fortune, in all. Display startling novelties, rise afresh like the sun every day. Change too the scene on which you shine, so that your loss may be felt in the old scenes of your triumph, while the novelty of your powers wins you applause in the new.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: George Sand by Nadar, 1864 · public domain
cards.qMean: Refresh your talents and image, like a phoenix rising again.
cards.qLife: An old brand redesigns its logo and suddenly feels new again.
cards.link: Playing a role well leads to the boldest move: writing your own role.

cards.chTitle: Re-Create Yourself
cards.title: In history: Caesar the actor
cards.text: Julius Caesar built his public self like a play: generous games, daring speeches, dramatic gestures like crossing the Rubicon. He refused to stay the man people expected. Emerson said the same in his own way: don't be trapped by what you were yesterday.
cards.quote: A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds
cards.qMean: Refusing to change just to stay consistent is small-minded.
cards.qLife: Changing your career path when you discover what you really love.
cards.orig: A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines. With consistency a great soul has simply nothing to do. He may as well concern himself with his shadow on the wall. Speak what you think now in hard words and to-morrow speak what to-morrow thinks in hard words again, though it contradict every thing you said to-day.—‘Ah, so you shall be sure to be misunderstood.’—Is it so bad then to be misunderstood? Pythagoras was misunderstood, and Socrates, and Jesus, and Luther, and Copernicus, and Galileo, and Newton, and every pure and wise spirit that ever took flesh. To be great is to be misunderstood.
cards.origFrom: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.qBy: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.cap: Gustave Boulanger, Jules-César arrivé au Rubicon, 1854, Musée Picardie · public domain

cards.chTitle: Keep Your Hands Clean
cards.title: Let others take the blame
cards.text: Leaders need to look clean even when hard things must happen. Historically, they used a scapegoat — like Cesare Borgia's harsh governor in the Romagna — or a go-between to carry unpopular tasks. Notice when you are being made someone's scapegoat.
cards.quote: princes ought to leave affairs of reproach to the management of others, and keep those of grace in their own hands.
cards.orig: Among the best ordered and governed kingdoms of our times is France, and in it are found many good institutions on which depend the liberty and security of the king; of these the first is the parliament and its authority, because he who founded the kingdom, knowing the ambition of the nobility and their boldness, considered that a bit to their mouths would be necessary to hold them in; and, on the other side, knowing the hatred of the people, founded in fear, against the nobles, he wished to protect them, yet he was not anxious for this to be the particular care of the king; therefore, to take away the reproach which he would be liable to from the nobles for favouring the people, and from the people for favouring the nobles, he set up an arbiter, who should be one who could beat down the great and favour the lesser without reproach to the king. Neither could you have a better or a more prudent arrangement, or a greater source of security to the king and kingdom. From this one can draw another important conclusion, that princes ought to leave affairs of reproach to the management of others, and keep those of grace in their own hands. And further, I consider that a prince ought to cherish the nobles, but not so as to make himself hated by the people.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Catarina de' Medici Uffizi · public domain
cards.qMean: Let others do the unpopular tasks; keep the pleasant ones yourself.
cards.qLife: The principal announces the trip; the vice-principal handles the detentions.
cards.link: A new self must stay spotless. Let others carry the dirt.

cards.chTitle: Keep Your Hands Clean
cards.title: In history: Borgia's scapegoat
cards.text: Cesare Borgia sent the brutal Remirro de Orco to tame the Romagna. When the people grew to hate the harshness, Borgia had Remirro cut in two and displayed in the square. The people were satisfied, and Borgia's hands looked clean.
cards.quote: The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed
cards.qMean: The cruel display both pleased and frightened the people.
cards.qLife: A company that fires one manager to take the blame for a scandal.
cards.orig: … and so, wishing to bring back peace and obedience to authority, he considered it necessary to give it a good governor. Thereupon he promoted Messer Ramiro d’Orco, a swift and cruel man, to whom he gave the fullest power. This man in a short time restored peace and unity with the greatest success. Afterwards the duke considered that it was not advisable to confer such excessive authority, for he had no doubt but that he would become odious, so he set up a court of judgment in the country, under a most excellent president, wherein all cities had their advocates. And because he knew that the past severity had caused some hatred against himself, so, to clear himself in the minds of the people, and gain them entirely to himself, he desired to show that, if any cruelty had been practised, it had not originated with him, but in the natural sternness of the minister. Under this pretence he took Ramiro, and one morning caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side. The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Cesena Rocca dei Malatesta · public domain

cards.chTitle: Play on People's Need to Believe to Create a Cultlike Following
cards.title: People want to believe
cards.text: Many people crave something to believe in. Charlatans in history gathered followers with vague, grand promises, rituals, and a sense of belonging. Recognising this pattern protects you from it.
cards.quote: the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it
cards.orig: For that reason, let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody; because the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it; and in the world there are only the vulgar, for the few find a place there only when the many have no ground to rest on.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Franz Anton Mesmer · public domain
cards.qMean: Most people are won over by appearances and results.
cards.qLife: Crowds trust the fancy-looking shop more than the plain one next door.
cards.link: With clean hands you can become something more: a figure people believe in.

cards.chTitle: Play on People's Need to Believe to Create a Cultlike Following
cards.title: In history: Mesmer's tubs
cards.text: Franz Mesmer claimed an invisible 'animal magnetism' could cure illness. In dim Paris salons, patients sat around tubs of iron filings while music played, and many felt better. A royal commission found no magnetism at all, only belief. Le Bon later wrote why it works.
cards.quote: The masses have never thirsted after truth.
cards.qMean: Crowds want something to believe in more than they want the truth.
cards.qLife: Viral miracle cures that spread despite no evidence.
cards.orig: Notwithstanding all its progress, philosophy has been unable as yet to offer the masses any ideal that can charm them; but, as they must have their illusions at all cost, they turn instinctively, as the insect seeks the light, to the rhetoricians who accord them what they want. Not truth, but error has always been the chief factor in the evolution of nations, and the reason why socialism is so powerful to-day is that it constitutes the last illusion that is still vital. In spite of all scientific demonstrations it continues on the increase. Its principal strength lies in the fact that it is championed by minds sufficiently ignorant of things as they are in reality to venture boldly to promise mankind happiness. The social illusion reigns to-day upon all the heaped-up ruins of the past, and to it belongs the future. The masses have never thirsted after truth. They turn aside from evidence that is not to their taste, preferring to deify error, if error seduce them. Whoever can supply them with illusions is easily their master; whoever attempts to destroy their illusions is always their victim.
cards.origFrom: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)
cards.qBy: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)
cards.cap: FREE mesmer painting · public domain

cards.chTitle: Enter Action with Boldness
cards.title: Hesitation is fatal
cards.text: Doubt shows, and it invites others to push back. Bold moves often succeed because they surprise and impress. If you act, act fully; timid half-measures get the worst of both worlds.
cards.quote: it is better to be adventurous than cautious
cards.orig: I conclude, therefore that, fortune being changeful and mankind steadfast in their ways, so long as the two are in agreement men are successful, but unsuccessful when they fall out. For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly. She is, therefore, always, woman-like, a lover of young men, because they are less cautious, more violent, and with more audacity command her.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Titian, Portrait of Pietro Aretino · public domain
cards.qMean: Taking bold risks usually beats being too cautious.
cards.qLife: The person who speaks first in the meeting sets the agenda.
cards.link: Belief follows confidence. Act boldly.

cards.chTitle: Enter Action with Boldness
cards.title: In history: selling the Eiffel Tower
cards.text: In 1925 the conman Victor Lustig, posing as a government official, persuaded scrap dealers that Paris was selling the Eiffel Tower. His sheer boldness made the story believable. He sold it, fled with the money, and almost sold it again.
cards.quote: While the hungry lion slumbers, not a deer comes to his den.
cards.qMean: Nothing comes to you if you just wait; you must act boldly.
cards.qLife: The job goes to the person who applied, not the one who meant to.
cards.orig:
"So verily,

"Worthy ends come not by wishing. Wouldst thou? Up, and win it, then! While the hungry lion slumbers, not a deer comes to his den."

Having concluded his reflections, the Raja gave orders to assemble a meeting of learned men. Then said he--

"Hear now, O my Pundits! Is there one among you so wise that he will undertake to give the second birth of Wisdom to these my sons, by teaching them the Books of Policy; for they have never yet read the Sacred Writings, and are altogether going in the wrong road; and ye know that

cards.chTitle: Plan All the Way to the End
cards.title: See the ending first
cards.text: Many plans fail because people only think about the start. Picture the full path — the obstacles, the reactions, the finish. Then you won't be surprised halfway, and you'll know when to stop.
cards.quote: the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won
cards.orig:
15. Thus it is that in war the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won, whereas he who is destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory.

16. The consummate leader cultivates the moral law, and strictly adheres to method and discipline; thus it is in his power to control success.

cards.qBy: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)

cards.qMean: The winner plans the victory before the fight; the loser fights hoping to win.
cards.qLife: Plan your route and parking before the job interview, not on the way.
cards.link: Boldness is not recklessness. Plan to the very end.

cards.chTitle: Plan All the Way to the End
cards.title: In history: Napoleon in Russia
cards.text: In 1812 Napoleon marched 600,000 men into Russia expecting a quick battle. The Russians retreated, burned the land, and let winter do the rest. Fewer than 100,000 came back. He had planned the beginning, not the end.
cards.quote: Thus do many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat: how much more no calculation at all!
cards.qMean: Careful planning wins; little planning loses.
cards.qLife: Starting a trek without checking the weather on the way down.
cards.orig:
26. Now the general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple ere the battle is fought.

The general who loses a battle makes but few calculations beforehand. Thus do many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat: how much more no calculation at all! It is by attention to this point that I can foresee who is likely to win or lose.

cards.chTitle: Make Your Accomplishments Seem Effortless
cards.title: Hide the sweat
cards.text: Showing how hard you worked makes your success look ordinary. Grace under pressure creates an illusion of natural talent. Practise in private; perform with ease in public.
cards.quote: What the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins, but excels in winning with ease.
cards.orig:
… to see sun and moon is no sign of sharp sight; to hear the noise of thunder is no sign of a quick ear.

11. What the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins, but excels in winning with ease.

12. Hence his victories bring him neither reputation for wisdom nor credit for courage.

13. He wins his battles by making no mistakes.

cards.qBy: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.cap: Houdini in Handcuffs, 1918 · public domain
cards.qMean: A clever fighter wins, and wins easily.
cards.qLife: The best students make exams look easy because they prepared for months.
cards.link: A planned victory should look effortless.

cards.chTitle: Make Your Accomplishments Seem Effortless
cards.title: In history: Houdini's secret work
cards.text: Harry Houdini's escapes looked like magic. Behind them were years of practising lock-picking, holding his breath and studying every handcuff made. Audiences saw effortless miracles because he hid the sweat.
cards.quote: It is useless to warn the student that he must be natural.
cards.qMean: You can't just tell someone to be natural; it comes from practice.
cards.qLife: A dancer whose effortless performance took thousands of hours.
cards.orig: It is useless to warn the student that he must be natural. To be natural may be to be monotonous. The little strawberry up in the arctics with a few tiny seeds and an acid tang is a natural berry, but it is not to be compared with the improved variety that we enjoy here. The dwarfed oak on the rocky hillside is natural, but a poor thing compared with the beautiful tree found in the rich, moist bottom lands. Be natural--but improve your natural gifts until you have approached the ideal, for we must strive after idealized nature, in fruit, tree, and speech.
cards.origFrom: J. B. Esenwein & Dale Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915)
cards.qBy: J. B. Esenwein & Dale Carnegie, The Art of Public Speaking (1915)
cards.cap: Houdini as ghostbuster (performance poster) · public domain

cards.chTitle: Control the Options: Get Others to Play with the Cards You Deal
cards.title: Choose the choices
cards.text: The best way to steer someone is to let them choose — between options you designed. They feel free, yet every path leads where you want. Watch for this in sales and politics.
cards.quote: By holding out advantages to him, he can cause the enemy to approach of his own accord

cards.qMean: Offer something attractive so the other side comes to you willingly.
cards.qLife: A shop's free samples draw people in without any advertising.
cards.link: Effortless control means choosing the choices others make.

cards.chTitle: Control the Options: Get Others to Play with the Cards You Deal
cards.title: In history: Ivan the Terrible's exit
cards.text: In 1564 Ivan IV suddenly left Moscow and threatened to abdicate. The terrified people and nobles begged him to return. He agreed, on his terms: unlimited power. They thought they were choosing; he had chosen for them.
cards.quote: the clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy
cards.qMean: The clever fighter makes the other side play his game.
cards.qLife: A parent who asks 'peas or carrots?' when vegetables were never optional.
cards.orig:
1. Sun Tzŭ said: Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy, will be fresh for the fight; whoever is second in the field and has to hasten to battle, will arrive exhausted.

2. Therefore the clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy, but does not allow the enemy’s will to be imposed on him.

3. By holding out advantages to him, he can cause the enemy to approach of his own accord; or, by inflicting damage, he can make it impossible for the enemy to draw near.

cards.chTitle: Play to People's Fantasies
cards.title: Sell the dream
cards.text: Plain truth is often dull and painful; fantasy is attractive. People are drawn to whoever promises a better story — instant wealth, a magic cure. This explains many famous frauds; it also explains why hope sells.
cards.quote: he who seeks to deceive will always find someone who will allow himself to be deceived.
cards.orig: But it is necessary to know well how to disguise this characteristic, and to be a great pretender and dissembler; and men are so simple, and so subject to present necessities, that he who seeks to deceive will always find someone who will allow himself to be deceived. One recent example I cannot pass over in silence. Alexander the Sixth did nothing else but deceive men, nor ever thought of doing otherwise, and he always found victims; for there never was a man who had greater power in asserting, or who with greater oaths would affirm a thing, yet would observe it less; nevertheless his deceits always succeeded according to his wishes, because he well understood this side of mankind.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Portret van Alessandro Cagliostro · public domain
cards.qMean: Anyone who wants to deceive will always find someone ready to believe.
cards.qLife: Scam messages work because a few people always click.
cards.link: People choose with their hopes. Speak to their fantasies.

cards.chTitle: Play to People's Fantasies
cards.title: In history: the Venetian alchemist
cards.text: In 1589 Bragadino arrived in bankrupt Venice claiming he could make gold. The desperate city gave him money and a palace. He kept delaying the miracle, until the truth came out. People wanted the dream too much to look closely, like Plato's prisoners watching shadows.
cards.quote: human beings living in an underground den which is open towards the light
cards.qMean: Plato pictures people trapped in a cave, seeing only shadows of reality.
cards.qLife: Believing an investment that promises to double your money in a month.
cards.orig: BOOK VII. And now I will describe in a figure the enlightenment or unenlightenment of our nature:—Imagine human beings living in an underground den which is open towards the light; they have been there from childhood, having their necks and legs chained, and can only see into the den. At a distance there is a fire, and between the fire and the prisoners a raised way, and a low wall is built along the way, like the screen over which marionette players show their puppets. Behind the wall appear moving figures, who hold in their hands various works of art, and among them images of men and animals, wood and stone, and some of the passers-by are talking and others silent. ‘A strange parable,’ he said, ‘and strange captives.’ They are ourselves, I replied; and they see only the shadows of the images which the fire throws on the wall of the den; to these they give names, and if we add an echo which returns from the wall, the voices of the passengers will seem to proceed from the shadows. Suppose now that you suddenly turn them round and make them look with pain and grief to themselves at the real images; …
cards.origFrom: Plato, The Republic (tr. Jowett)
cards.qBy: Plato, The Republic (tr. Jowett)

cards.title: Find the lever
cards.text: Everyone has a soft spot — an insecurity, a need, a secret pleasure. Find it and you know how to move them. The phrase comes straight from the 17th-century Spanish writer Baltasar Gracián.
cards.quote: Find out each Man's Thumbscrew. 'Tis the art of setting their wills in action.

AJ] men are idolaters, some of fame, others of self-interest, most of pleasure. Skill consists in knowing these idols in order to bring them into play. Knowing any man’s main-

cards.qLife: One colleague wants praise, another wants time off — reward each differently.
cards.link: Every fantasy hides a weakness: find each person's lever.

cards.chTitle: Discover Each Man's Thumbscrew
cards.title: In history: Richelieu's lever
cards.text: Cardinal Richelieu rose by finding what the queen mother, Marie de' Medici, craved: flattery and power for herself. He gave her both, became indispensable, then used her son, Louis XIII, to push her aside. Machiavelli knew where people are most sensitive.
cards.quote: men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony
cards.qMean: People forgive a parent's death sooner than losing their property.
cards.qLife: Touch someone's savings and you'll see how strongly they react.
cards.orig: Nevertheless a prince ought to inspire fear in such a way that, if he does not win love, he avoids hatred; because he can endure very well being feared whilst he is not hated, which will always be as long as he abstains from the property of his citizens and subjects and from their women. But when it is necessary for him to proceed against the life of someone, he must do it on proper justification and for manifest cause, but above all things he must keep his hands off the property of others, because men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony. Besides, pretexts for taking away the property are never wanting; for he who has once begun to live by robbery will always find pretexts for seizing what belongs to others; but reasons for taking life, on the contrary, are more difficult to find and sooner lapse. But when a prince is with his army, and has under control a multitude of soldiers, then it is quite necessary for him to disregard the reputation of cruelty, for without it he would never hold his army united or disposed to its duties.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)

cards.chTitle: Be Royal in Your Own Fashion: Act Like a King to Be Treated Like One
cards.title: Carry yourself like royalty
cards.text: How you carry yourself teaches others how to treat you. Calm dignity and quiet confidence make people respect you. Act cheap or desperate and you will be treated that way.
cards.quote: Let each deed of a man in its degree, though he be not a king, be worthy of a prince
cards.orig: Let each deed of a man in its degree, though he be not a king, be worthy of a prince, and let his action be princely within due limits. Sublime in action, lofty in thought, in all things like a king, at least in merit if not in might. For true kingship lies in spotless rectitude, and he need not envy greatness who can serve as a model of it. Especially should those near the throne aim at true superiority, and prefer to share the true qualities of royalty rather than take parts in its mere ceremonies, yet without. affecting its imperfections but sharing in its true dignity.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Portrait of a Man, Said to be Christopher Columbus · public domain
cards.qMean: Act with dignity, as if you were royalty, whatever your rank.
cards.qLife: A waiter who carries himself with pride gets more respect than a sloppy manager.
cards.link: Use levers quietly, and carry yourself like royalty.

cards.chTitle: Be Royal in Your Own Fashion: Act Like a King to Be Treated Like One
cards.title: In history: Columbus asks for titles
cards.text: Before sailing, Christopher Columbus, a poor sailor's son, demanded to be made Admiral of the Ocean Sea, viceroy of any lands he found, and to receive a tenth of all riches. Ferdinand and Isabella agreed, partly because he asked as if it were obvious.
cards.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
cards.qMean: Believe in yourself; everyone responds to that.
cards.qLife: Asking for the salary you're worth instead of apologising for it.
cards.orig: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Accept the place the divine providence has found for you, the society of your contemporaries, the connection of events. Great men have always done so, and confided themselves childlike to the genius of their age, betraying their perception that the absolutely trustworthy was seated at their heart, working through their hands, predominating in all their being. And we are now men, and must accept in the highest mind the same transcendent destiny; and not minors and invalids in a protected corner, not cowards fleeing before a revolution, but guides, redeemers and benefactors, obeying the Almighty effort and advancing on Chaos and the Dark.
cards.origFrom: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.qBy: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.cap: Emanuel Gottlieb Leutze - Columbus Before the Queen · public domain

cards.chTitle: Master the Art of Timing
cards.title: Wait, then strike
cards.text: Never seem in a hurry — haste shows you are not in control. Be patient while the moment ripens, then move fast. Fouché, Napoleon's police chief, survived every regime in France by reading the times.
cards.quote: Time and I against any two.
cards.orig: It’s a sign of a noble heart dowered with patience, never to be in a hurry, never to be in a passion. First be master over yourself if you would be master over others. You must pass through the circumference of time before arriving at the centre of opportunity. A wise reserve seasons the aims and matures the means. Time’s crutch effects more than the iron club of Hercules. God Himself chasteneth not with a rod but with time. He}? spake a great word who said, “Time and I against any two.”
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Rembrandt - Quintus Fabius Maximus · public domain
cards.qMean: Patience and time can beat any two opponents.
cards.qLife: Waiting for a sale instead of buying at full price.
cards.link: Royal dignity includes patience. Master timing.

cards.chTitle: Master the Art of Timing
cards.title: In history: Fouché the survivor
cards.text: Joseph Fouché served the Revolution, Napoleon and the returning king, switching sides at exactly the right moment each time. He survived what killed almost everyone else. His secret was waiting until the tide had clearly turned, then moving fast.
cards.quote: Energy may be likened to the bending of a crossbow; decision, to the releasing of the trigger.
cards.qMean: Build up patiently, then act decisively at the right moment.
cards.qLife: Waiting for the right moment to ask for a raise, then asking clearly.
cards.orig:
14. Therefore the good fighter will be terrible in his onset, and prompt in his decision.

15. Energy may be likened to the bending of a crossbow; decision, to the releasing of the trigger.

16. Amid the turmoil and tumult of battle, there may be seeming disorder and yet no real disorder at all; amid confusion and chaos, your array may be without head or tail, yet it will be proof against defeat.

cards.chTitle: Disdain Things You Cannot Have: Ignoring Them Is the Best Revenge
cards.title: Shrug it off
cards.text: Reacting to a small irritation makes it bigger and shows it hurt you. Often the most powerful response is to seem not to care. Attention is fuel — starve trivial attacks of it.
cards.quote: Fools depreciate all men
cards.orig: There is none who cannot teach somebody something, and there is none so excellent but he is excelled. ‘To know how to make use of every one is useful knowledge. Wise men appreciate all men, for they see the good in each and know how hard it is to make anything good. Fools depreciate all men, not recognising the good and selecting the bad.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: After Hans Holbein the Younger - Portrait of Henry VIII · public domain
cards.qMean: Foolish people look down on everyone.
cards.qLife: A troll mocking everything online shows only their own emptiness.
cards.link: Some things will never be yours. Act as if you don't want them.

cards.chTitle: Disdain Things You Cannot Have: Ignoring Them Is the Best Revenge
cards.title: In history: the fox and the grapes
cards.text: Aesop's fox couldn't reach the grapes, so he walked off saying they were sour anyway. The fable mocks him, but the law takes him seriously: showing you don't care about what you can't have robs it of its power over you. Epictetus said our troubles come from how we see things.
cards.quote: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
cards.qMean: It's our opinions about things, not the things themselves, that upset us.
cards.qLife: Losing a game feels smaller once you decide it was just a game.
cards.orig: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things. Thus death is nothing terrible, else it would have appeared so to Socrates. But the terror consists in our notion of death, that it is terrible. When, therefore, we are hindered or disturbed, or grieved, let us never impute it to others, but to ourselves—that is, to our own views. It is the action of an uninstructed person to reproach others for his own misfortunes; of one entering upon instruction, to reproach himself; and one perfectly instructed, to reproach neither others nor himself.
cards.origFrom: Epictetus, The Enchiridion (tr. Higginson)
cards.qBy: Epictetus, The Enchiridion (tr. Higginson)
cards.cap: Fable of the lioness and the fox LCCN2005692044 · public domain

cards.chTitle: Create Compelling Spectacles
cards.title: Put on a show
cards.text: Images and symbols move people more than arguments. Louis XIV made himself the 'Sun King', staging his whole life at Versailles like a theatre. A striking show creates awe and silences doubt.
cards.quote: Nothing makes a prince so much esteemed as great enterprises and setting a fine example.
cards.orig: Nothing makes a prince so much esteemed as great enterprises and setting a fine example. We have in our time Ferdinand of Aragon, the present King of Spain. He can almost be called a new prince, because he has risen, by fame and glory, from being an insignificant king to be the foremost king in Christendom; and if you will consider his deeds you will find them all great and some of them extraordinary. In the beginning of his reign he attacked Granada, and this enterprise was the foundation of his dominions. He did this quietly at first and without any fear of hindrance, for he held the minds of the barons of Castile occupied in thinking of the war and not anticipating any innovations; thus they did not perceive that by these means he was acquiring power and authority over them. He was able with the money of the Church and of the people to sustain his armies, and by that long war to lay the foundation for the military skill which has since distinguished him. Further, always using religion as a plea, so as to undertake greater schemes, he devoted himself with pious cruelty to driving out and clearing his kingdom of the Moors; …
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Ballet de la nuit 1653 · public domain
cards.qMean: Big projects and good examples earn the most respect.
cards.qLife: A mayor who builds a bridge is remembered more than one who gives speeches.
cards.link: Instead of chasing, create a spectacle people come to see.

cards.chTitle: Create Compelling Spectacles
cards.title: In history: Cleopatra's barge
cards.text: When Mark Antony summoned Cleopatra, she came up the river on a golden barge with purple sails and silver oars, dressed as Venus, with perfume drifting to the shore. Antony was conquered before they spoke. Crowds, Le Bon wrote, are moved by images, not reasons.
cards.quote: allows himself to be impressed by words and images
cards.qMean: People in crowds are swayed by striking words and pictures.
cards.qLife: A brilliant product launch that people remember more than the product.
cards.orig: Moreover, by the mere fact that he forms part of an organised crowd, a man descends several rungs in the ladder of civilisation. Isolated, he may be a cultivated individual; in a crowd, he is a barbarian--that is, a creature acting by instinct. He possesses the spontaneity, the violence, the ferocity, and also the enthusiasm and heroism of primitive beings, whom he further tends to resemble by the facility with which he allows himself to be impressed by words and images--which would be entirely without action on each of the isolated individuals composing the crowd--and to be induced to commit acts contrary to his most obvious interests and his best-known habits. An individual in a crowd is a grain of sand amid other grains of sand, which the wind stirs up at will.
cards.origFrom: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)
cards.qBy: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)

cards.chTitle: Think as You Like but Behave Like Others
cards.title: Blend in outside
cards.text: Showing off unusual opinions or habits makes others feel judged. Keep your most radical thoughts for trusted friends, and speak like the people around you in public. You keep freedom of thought without making enemies.
cards.quote: Think with the Few and speak with the Many.
cards.orig:
It is a secret force of superiority not to have to get on by artful trickery but by an inborn power of rule. All submit to it without knowing why, recognising the secret vigour of connatural authority. Such magisterial spirits are kings by merit and lions by innate privilege. By the esteem which they inspire, they hold the hearts and minds of the rest. If their other qualities permit, such men are born to be the prime motors of the state. ‘They perform more by a gesture than others by a long harangue.

xliii Think with the Few and speak with the Many.

By swimming against the stream it is impossible to remove error, easy to fall into .

cards.qMean: Think freely with a few trusted people; talk like everyone else in public.
cards.qLife: Share your wild business idea with close friends, not the whole family WhatsApp.
cards.link: Stand out in display, but blend in with your opinions.

cards.chTitle: Think as You Like but Behave Like Others
cards.title: In history: Socrates' trial
cards.text: Socrates questioned everyone in Athens and openly mocked its customs. In 399 BC the city tried him for corrupting the young and executed him. Wise people since have learned to keep their most unusual thoughts to themselves.
cards.quote: He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
cards.qMean: Those who truly understand rarely talk about it; those who talk the most understand least.
cards.qLife: The person bragging loudest at a party usually knows the least.

cards.title: Stay calm, unsettle them
cards.text: Angry people make mistakes. Keep your temper, and notice when someone is trying to provoke you. Losing control hands the advantage to the calmer side.

cards.chTitle: Stir Up Waters to Catch Fish
cards.title: In history: Fabius the delayer
cards.text: Hannibal tried every trick to provoke the Roman general Fabius into battle: insults, burned farms, feigned retreats. Fabius refused, shadowing him patiently. Hannibal's angry frustration, not Roman swords, slowly wore his army down. Darwin noticed that giving way to anger only feeds it.
cards.quote: He who gives way to violent gestures will increase his rage
cards.qMean: Acting out anger makes you angrier.
cards.qLife: Shouting back in an argument only makes both people madder.
cards.orig: … Whatever amount of truth the so-called science of physiognomy may contain, appears to depend, as Haller long ago remarked, on different persons bringing into frequent use different facial muscles, according to their dispositions; the development of these muscles being perhaps thus increased, and the lines or furrows on the face, due to their habitual contraction, being thus rendered deeper and more conspicuous. The free expression by outward signs of an emotion intensifies it. On the other hand, the repression, as far as this is possible, of all outward signs softens our emotions. He who gives way to violent gestures will increase his rage; he who does not control the signs of fear will experience fear in a greater degree; and he who remains passive when overwhelmed with grief loses his best chance of recovering elasticity of mind. These results follow partly from the intimate relation which exists between almost all the emotions and their outward manifestations; and partly from the direct influence of exertion on the heart, and consequently on the brain. …
cards.origFrom: Charles Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions (1872)

cards.chTitle: Despise the Free Lunch
cards.title: Nothing is free
cards.text: What comes free often carries a hidden cost — obligation, guilt, strings attached. Paying your own way keeps you independent. Generosity, used wisely, wins goodwill.
cards.quote: What costs little is little worth.
cards.orig: There is no attaining eminence without both, and where they unite there is the greatest eminence. Mediocrity obtains more with application than superiority without it. Work is the price which is paid for reputation. What costs little is little worth. Even for the highest posts it is only in some cases application that is wanting, rarely the talent. Tio prefer moderate success in great things than eminence in a humble post has the excuse of a generous mind, but not so to be content with humble mediocrity when you could shine among the highest. ‘Thus nature and art are both needed, and application sets on them the seal.

cards.qMean: Things that cost nothing are usually worth little.
cards.qLife: The free gym trial nobody uses versus the paid membership people actually go to.
cards.link: Unsettled people grab at free things. Be wary of anything free.

cards.title: In history: the Trojan Horse
cards.text: After ten years of war, the Greeks left a giant wooden horse as a gift and sailed away. The Trojans dragged it inside their walls. That night Greek soldiers climbed out and opened the gates. The free gift cost Troy everything. Money and gifts, the Hitopadesha warns, change how people treat you.
cards.quote: Wealth is friends, home, father, brother
cards.qMean: Money brings friends, family and respect, which is why it's dangerous.
cards.qLife: A 'free' trial that quietly signs you up for a yearly plan.

'Wealth is friends, home, father, brother--title to respect and fame; Yea, and wealth is held for wisdom--that it should be so is shame,' 'Home is empty to the childless; hearts to them who friends deplore:-- Earth unto the idle-minded; and the three worlds to the poor.'

'I can stay here no longer; and to tell my distress to another is out of the question--altogether out of the question!--

cards.chTitle: Avoid Stepping into a Great Man's Shoes
cards.title: Make your own name
cards.text: Following a famous predecessor is a trap: everything you do gets compared to a legend. Create your own space and style instead of copying theirs. Alexander the Great feared his father Philip would leave him nothing to conquer.
cards.quote: It is no great gain if a poor successor makes the predecessor seem good
cards.orig: Few reach such favour with the many ; if with the wise ’tis the height of happiness. When one has finished one’s work, coldness is the general rule. But there are ways of earning this reward of goodwill. .The sure way Is to excel in your office and talents: add to this agreeable manner and you reach the point where you become necessary to your office, not your office to you. Some do honour to their post, with others ’tis the other way. It is no great gain if a poor successor makes the predecessor seem good, for this does not imply that the one is missed, but that & other is wished away.
