cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Alexander the Great mosaic · public domain
cards.qMean: It's no honour if you only look good because a weak successor follows you.
cards.qLife: A coach who leaves a team in chaos isn't great just because the next coach is worse.
cards.link: Gifts and inheritances bind you. So does a great man's name.

cards.chTitle: Avoid Stepping into a Great Man's Shoes
cards.title: In history: Alexander and Philip
cards.text: Alexander the Great grew up in the shadow of his father Philip, who had already conquered Greece. He reportedly complained that his father would leave him nothing to win. So he went further, to Persia, Egypt and India, and made a name bigger than Philip's.
cards.quote: Whoso would be a man, must be a nonconformist.
cards.qMean: To be your own person you must not just follow the crowd, or your parents.
cards.qLife: Choosing your own career instead of the family business.
cards.orig: Whoso would be a man, must be a nonconformist. He who would gather immortal palms must not be hindered by the name of goodness, but must explore if it be goodness. Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind. Absolve you to yourself, and you shall have the suffrage of the world. I remember an answer which when quite young I was prompted to make to a valued adviser who was wont to importune me with the dear old doctrines of the church. On my saying, “What have I to do with the sacredness of traditions, if I live wholly from within?” my friend suggested,—“But these impulses may be from below, not from above.” I replied, “They do not seem to me to be such; but if I am the Devil’s child, I will live then from the Devil.” No law can be sacred to me but that of my nature. Good and bad are but names very readily transferable to that or this; the only right is what is after my constitution; the only wrong what is against it. A man is to carry himself in the presence of all opposition as if every thing were titular and ephemeral but he. …
cards.origFrom: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.qBy: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.cap: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic · public domain

cards.chTitle: Strike the Shepherd, and the Sheep Will Scatter
cards.title: Find the source
cards.text: Trouble in a group often grows from one person — a schemer, a ringleader. Remove or win over that one source, and the rest settles. Don't waste effort on the followers.
cards.quote: Begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will.

18. If asked how to cope with a great host of the enemy in orderly array and on the point of marching to the attack, I should say: "Begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will."

19. Rapidity is the essence of war:

cards.chTitle: Strike the Shepherd, and the Sheep Will Scatter
cards.title: In history: the crowd's leader
cards.text: Athenians sometimes held an 'ostracism': each citizen scratched on a pottery shard the name of the man they most wanted gone, and the top name was exiled for ten years. Remove the leader and the faction falls apart. Le Bon explains why crowds depend on their leaders.
cards.quote: by the mere fact that he forms part of an organised crowd, a man descends several rungs in the ladder of civilisation
cards.qMean: In a crowd, a person thinks less for themselves.
cards.qLife: A rowdy group of fans calms down when its loudest member leaves.
cards.orig: Moreover, by the mere fact that he forms part of an organised crowd, a man descends several rungs in the ladder of civilisation. Isolated, he may be a cultivated individual; in a crowd, he is a barbarian--that is, a creature acting by instinct. He possesses the spontaneity, the violence, the ferocity, and also the enthusiasm and heroism of primitive beings, whom he further tends to resemble by the facility with which he allows himself to be impressed by words and images--which would be entirely without action on each of the isolated individuals composing the crowd--and to be induced to commit acts contrary to his most obvious interests and his best-known habits. An individual in a crowd is a grain of sand amid other grains of sand, which the wind stirs up at will.
cards.origFrom: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)
cards.qBy: Gustave Le Bon, The Crowd (1895)

cards.chTitle: Work on the Hearts and Minds of Others
cards.title: Win their hearts
cards.text: Force makes people resentful; persuasion makes them loyal. Learn what people feel and value, and speak to that. People who feel understood follow willingly.
cards.quote: it is necessary for a prince to have the people friendly, otherwise he has no security in adversity.
cards.orig: Therefore, one who becomes a prince through the favour of the people ought to keep them friendly, and this he can easily do seeing they only ask not to be oppressed by him. But one who, in opposition to the people, becomes a prince by the favour of the nobles, ought, above everything, to seek to win the people over to himself, and this he may easily do if he takes them under his protection. Because men, when they receive good from him of whom they were expecting evil, are bound more closely to their benefactor; thus the people quickly become more devoted to him than if he had been raised to the principality by their favours; and the prince can win their affections in many ways, but as these vary according to the circumstances one cannot give fixed rules, so I omit them; but, I repeat, it is necessary for a prince to have the people friendly, otherwise he has no security in adversity.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Louise Elisabeth Vigée-Lebrun - Marie-Antoinette de Lorraine-Habsbourg, reine de France et ses enfants · public domain
cards.qMean: A leader needs the people on his side or he has no safety in bad times.
cards.qLife: A brand loved by its customers survives a bad product launch.
cards.link: Force wins battles; hearts win wars.

cards.chTitle: Work on the Hearts and Minds of Others
cards.title: In history: Akbar wins hearts
cards.text: The Mughal emperor Akbar conquered by the sword, but he held his empire by winning hearts: he married Rajput princesses, abolished the tax on non-Muslims and welcomed scholars of every faith to debate at his court. Tiruvalluvar's way is gentler still.
cards.quote: Let him do them a good turn and make them ashamed in their hearts.
cards.qMean: Answer people who hurt you with kindness.
cards.qLife: Helping a neighbour who once complained about you.
cards.orig:
313. If thou injure another, even though it be only a man who hath injured thee without any provocation, thou simply bringest down upon thyself evils that can never be remedied.

314. How shall a man punish them that have injured him ? Let him do them a good turn and make them ashamed in their hearts.

315. Of what avail is intelligence to a man if he doth not look on others’ pain as his own and abstain from injuring any ?

cards.chTitle: Disarm and Infuriate with the Mirror Effect
cards.title: Mirror them
cards.text: Reflecting someone's behaviour back at them is powerful: it can calm them by showing you understand, or unsettle them by showing them their own tactics. Mirroring builds rapport — and it can also be a weapon.
cards.quote: Success in warfare is gained by carefully accommodating ourselves to the enemy's purpose.
cards.orig:
58. Place your army in deadly peril, and it will survive; plunge it into desperate straits, and it will come off in safety.

59. For it is precisely when a force has fallen into harm’s way that is capable of striking a blow for victory.

60. Success in warfare is gained by carefully accommodating ourselves to the enemy’s purpose.

61. By persistently hanging on the enemy’s flank,

we shall succeed in the long run

cards.chTitle: Disarm and Infuriate with the Mirror Effect
cards.title: In history: Diogenes and Alexander
cards.text: Alexander the Great found the philosopher Diogenes lying in the sun and asked what he could do for him. 'Stand out of my sunlight,' said Diogenes. Alexander, used to flattery, saw his own pride reflected back. Emerson's mirror is a kinder one.
cards.quote: the only way to have a friend is to be one.
cards.qMean: To have friends, be a good friend first.
cards.qLife: Being the first to say hello in a new class.
cards.orig: … Let us not interfere. Who set you to cast about what you should say to the select souls, or how to say any thing to such? No matter how ingenious, no matter how graceful and bland. There are innumerable degrees of folly and wisdom, and for you to say aught is to be frivolous. Wait, and thy heart shall speak. Wait until the necessary and everlasting overpowers you, until day and night avail themselves of your lips. The only reward of virtue is virtue; the only way to have a friend is to be one. You shall not come nearer a man by getting into his house. If unlike, his soul only flees the faster from you, and you shall never catch a true glance of his eye. We see the noble afar off and they repel us; why should we intrude? Late,—very late,—we perceive that no arrangements, no introductions, no consuetudes or habits of society would be of any avail to establish us in such relations with them as we desire,—but solely the uprise of nature in us to the same degree it is in them; then shall we meet as water with water; and if we should not meet them then, we shall not want them, for we are already they. …
cards.origFrom: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.qBy: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series (1841)
cards.cap: Caspar de Crayer Alexander and Diogenes · public domain

cards.chTitle: Preach the Need for Change, but Never Reform Too Much at Once
cards.title: Change slowly
cards.text: People say they want change but cling to familiar habits. Reform too fast and you create a backlash. Wrap new ideas in old, comforting forms, and move step by step.
cards.quote: there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things
cards.orig: Those who by valorous ways become princes, like these men, acquire a principality with difficulty, but they keep it with ease. The difficulties they have in acquiring it rise in part from the new rules and methods which they are forced to introduce to establish their government and its security. And it ought to be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things, because the innovator has for enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new. This coolness arises partly from fear of the opponents, who have the laws on their side, and partly from the incredulity of men, who do not readily believe in new things until they have had a long experience of them. Thus it happens that whenever those who are hostile have the opportunity to attack they do it like partisans, whilst the others defend lukewarmly, in such wise that the prince is endangered along with them.
cards.origFrom: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.qBy: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
cards.cap: Cromwell,Thomas(1EEssex)01 · public domain
cards.qMean: Introducing a new way of doing things is the hardest, riskiest task.
cards.qLife: Changing the family's holiday tradition meets more resistance than you'd expect.
cards.link: Mirrors unsettle. So does too much change at once.

cards.chTitle: Preach the Need for Change, but Never Reform Too Much at Once
cards.title: In history: Cromwell's revolution
cards.text: Thomas Cromwell rushed through huge changes for Henry VIII: closing the monasteries, rewriting church law. The speed made enemies everywhere, and when the king turned on him, no one defended him. He was executed in 1540. Lao Tzu's advice on governing is to handle things gently.
cards.quote: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
cards.qMean: Govern gently, without stirring too much, or things fall apart.
cards.qLife: A new manager who changes everything in week one usually faces a revolt.
cards.orig:
60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.

2. Let the kingdom be governed according to the Tao, and the manes of the departed will not manifest their spiritual energy. It is not that those manes have not that spiritual energy, but it will not be employed to hurt men. It is not that it could not hurt men, but neither does the ruling sage hurt them.

cards.chTitle: Never Appear Too Perfect
cards.title: Show a small flaw
cards.text: Seeming flawless makes others envious and suspicious. A small, harmless weakness makes you human and likable. In ancient Athens, people even voted to exile a man partly because they were tired of hearing him called 'the Just' — ostracism.
cards.quote: Allow Yourself some venial Fault. Some such carelessness is often the greatest recommendation of talent.
cards.orig:
A sage once reduced all virtue to the golden mean. Push right to the extreme and it becomes wrong: press all the juice from an orange and it becomes bitter. Even in enjoyment never go to extremes. ‘Thought too subtle is dull. If you milk a cow too much you draw blood, not milk.

Ixxxiii Allow Yourself some venial Fault.

Some such carelessness is often the greatest recommendation of talent. For envy exercises ostracism, most envenomed when most polite. It counts it to perfection as a failing that it has no faults ; for being perfect in all it condemns

cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)

cards.qMean: Allow yourself a small harmless flaw; it makes your talent less threatening.
cards.qLife: The brilliant new colleague who admits she can't park is liked more.
cards.link: Change slowly, and don't look perfect while you do it.

cards.chTitle: Never Appear Too Perfect
cards.title: In history: Cosimo's modesty
cards.text: Cosimo de' Medici, richest man in Florence, wore plain clothes, built modest houses and rejected a grand palace design as too showy. He ruled the city for thirty years without a title, and people let him. Nietzsche said every deep mind needs a mask.
cards.quote: Every profound spirit needs a mask
cards.qMean: Deep people need to hide parts of themselves.
cards.qLife: A brilliant student who doesn't brag about grades keeps more friends.
cards.orig: … I could imagine that a man with something costly and fragile to conceal, would roll through life clumsily and rotundly like an old, green, heavily-hooped wine-cask: the refinement of his shame requiring it to be so. A man who has depths in his shame meets his destiny and his delicate decisions upon paths which few ever reach, and with regard to the existence of which his nearest and most intimate friends may be ignorant; his mortal danger conceals itself from their eyes, and equally so his regained security. Such a hidden nature, which instinctively employs speech for silence and concealment, and is inexhaustible in evasion of communication, DESIRES and insists that a mask of himself shall occupy his place in the hearts and heads of his friends; and supposing he does not desire it, his eyes will some day be opened to the fact that there is nevertheless a mask of him there--and that it is well to be so. Every profound spirit needs a mask; nay, more, around every profound spirit there continually grows a mask, owing to the constantly false, that is to say, SUPERFICIAL interpretation of every word he utters, every step he takes, every sign of life he manifests.
cards.origFrom: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil (tr. Zimmern, 1907)
cards.qBy: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil (tr. Zimmern, 1907)
cards.cap: Pontormo - Ritratto di Cosimo il Vecchio · public domain

cards.chTitle: Do Not Go Past the Mark You Aimed For; In Victory, Learn When to Stop
cards.title: Know when to stop
cards.text: Success can make people complacent and greedy. After a win, pause and consolidate. Many have lost everything by pushing their luck one step too far.
cards.quote: Leave your Luck while Winning. All the best players do it. A fine retreat is as good as a gallant attack.
cards.orig:
… xxxvili Leave your Luck while Winning.

All the best players do it. A fine retreat is as good as a gallant attack. Bring your exploits under cover when there are enough, or even when there are many of them. Luck long lasting was ever suspicious ; interrupted seems safer, and is even sweeter to the taste for a little infusion of bitter-sweet. The higher the heap of luck, the greater the risk of a slip, and down comes all. Fortune pays you sometimes for the intensity of her favours by the shortness of their duration. She soon tires of carrying any one long on her shoulders.
cards.origFrom: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.qBy: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647, tr. Jacobs)
cards.cap: Croesus at the Stake, after Hans Holbein the Younger · public domain
cards.qMean: Quit while you're winning; a good retreat is as good as a bold attack.
cards.qLife: Leave the casino after a win instead of betting it all again.
cards.link: Imperfection keeps you human. Knowing when to stop keeps you safe.

cards.chTitle: Do Not Go Past the Mark You Aimed For; In Victory, Learn When to Stop
cards.title: In history: Croesus goes too far
cards.text: Croesus of Lydia, the richest king alive, asked the oracle whether to attack Persia. 'You will destroy a great empire,' it said. He attacked, and destroyed his own. He should have stopped while ahead. Epictetus' rule: take your modest share, as at a banquet.
cards.quote: Remember that you must behave as at a banquet.
cards.qMean: Take your fair share politely, don't grab everything.
cards.qLife: Leaving the game while you're winning instead of betting it all.
cards.orig: Remember that you must behave as at a banquet. Is anything brought round to you? Put out your hand and take a moderate share. Does it pass by you? Do not stop it. Is it not yet come? Do not yearn in desire toward it, but wait till it reaches you. So with regard to children, wife, office, riches; and you will some time or other be worthy to feast with the gods. And if you do not so much as take the things which are set before you, but are able even to forego them, then you will not only be worthy to feast with the gods, but to rule with them also. For, by thus doing, Diogenes and Heraclitus, and others like them, deservedly became divine, and were so recognized.
cards.origFrom: Epictetus, The Enchiridion (tr. Higginson)
cards.qBy: Epictetus, The Enchiridion (tr. Higginson)
cards.cap: Kroisos stake Louvre G197 · public domain

cards.chTitle: Assume Formlessness
cards.title: Be like water
cards.text: Rigid people and rigid plans break. Stay flexible, adapt to circumstances, and avoid being pinned down. The old image is water — it fits any container and wears away stone.
cards.quote: Military tactics are like unto water; for water in its natural course runs away from high places and hastens downwards.
cards.orig:
28. Do not repeat the tactics which have gained you one victory, but let your methods be regulated by the infinite variety of circumstances.

29. Military tactics are like unto water; for water in its natural course runs away from high places and hastens downwards.

30. So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong and to strike at what is weak.
cards.origFrom: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.qBy: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War (tr. Giles, 1910)
cards.cap: Tsunami by hokusai 19th century · public domain
cards.qMean: Be flexible like water, flowing around obstacles.
cards.qLife: When a road is blocked, a good driver takes side streets instead of waiting.
cards.link: The last law sums up all the rest: stay fluid.

cards.chTitle: Assume Formlessness
cards.title: In history: the Mongol horsemen
cards.text: Genghis Khan's armies had no cities to defend and no slow supply wagons. They moved fast, split up, joined again and appeared where no one expected. Fixed walls and heavy armies could not hold them. Water, in the Tao Te Ching, is the model.
cards.quote: The highest excellence is like (that of) water.
cards.qMean: The best way to be is like water: flexible and patient.
cards.qLife: A startup that pivots quickly while big companies are stuck.
cards.orig:
8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.

2. The excellence of a residence is in (the suitability of) the place; that of the mind is in abysmal stillness; that of associations is in their being with the virtuous; that of government is in its securing good order; that of (the conduct of) affairs is in its ability; and that of (the initiation of) any movement is in its timeliness.
